## Before submitting

- [ ] I agree to license this contribution under the terms of [LICENSE.txt](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/develop/LICENSE.txt).
- [x] I ran `pre-commit run` and committed any formatting changes. (black, black-jupyter, SPDX header passed; clang-format had no files.)
- [x] I reviewed the Hard Rules in the `AGENTS.md` for each directory this PR touches (see [root AGENTS.md § Reviewing a PR](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/develop/AGENTS.md#reviewing-a-pr-human-or-agent)) and my changes comply, or I explain the exception below.
- [ ] I added GitHub labels: one `cat-*`, one or more `area:*` / `op:*`, and one `orig-*` (see [label list](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/labels)). (Proposed: the performance `cat-*` label, `op: DSA`, `area:sparse_attention`, `orig-nv-eng`; to be checked against the label list when opening.)

## Affected area

FE OSS kernels or CuTeDSL (DSA `indexer_top_k` radix kernel and its scratch sizing).

## Summary

`indexer_top_k` on BF16 rows wider than 32,768 columns now bins its coarse histogram with the same FP16-derived key the FP32 path uses, so BF16 top-k is no longer slower than FP32 on long rows.

- `IndexerTopKKernelVarlen`: new `bf16_fp16_coarse_key` (BF16 and `max_num_cols > 32768`, via `bf16_uses_fp16_coarse_key()`). For those specializations `to_coarse_key` converts BF16 -> FP32 -> FP16 and takes the FP16 top byte (sign + 5 exponent + 2 mantissa bits), exactly as FP32 does. The fine key stays the exact 16-bit BF16 key; because a coarse bin no longer fixes its top byte, the refine covers both bytes in two rounds (`first_refine_shift = 8`, `num_refine_rounds = 2`), which alternate between two candidate buffers like FP32's four rounds (`num_buffer_smem_input_idx = 2`).
- `buffer_numbers(torch_dtype, num_cols=None)`: new trailing `num_cols`; 2 int32 scratch rows per input row for FP32 and for BF16 wider than 32,768 columns, else 1 (`None` returns the dtype's maximum). `IndexerTopK` passes its `num_cols`, so `scratch_workspace_bytes()` follows; `benchmark/dsa/benchmark_deterministic_top_k.py` updated the same way.
- Unchanged: FP32, FP16, and BF16 up to 32,768 columns (same coarse key, rounds, buffers and scratch). Up to that width every candidate fits the single shared-memory buffer of the native BF16 key, and on SM120 the 99 KiB block budget holds only that one buffer there (wider BF16 already takes the small-buffer large-occupancy specialization on SM120, so the second buffer costs at most 16 KiB of shared memory).
- Docs: `docs/fe-oss-apis/dsa.md` workspace formula.

## Why

The radix top-k histograms an 8-bit coarse key, collects every candidate of the threshold bin (shared memory first, then the global scratch), and refines them with the exact key. For FP32 the coarse key is the FP16 top byte, a quarter binade per bin. For BF16 it was the BF16 top byte, sign + 7 exponent bits, i.e. two binades per bin. Scores concentrated in a few binades (indexer scores, Gaussian-like data) then put a large share of a long row into the threshold bin: a CPU model of the GLM-5.2 indexer score distribution gives 7K to 90K threshold-bin candidates per 1M-key row with the BF16 key versus 2.5K to 6.3K with the FP16-derived key. Those candidates spill to the global scratch and are gathered again in the refine round.

At GLM-5.2 1M-token context (CP64, rank 0: 16384 rows x 1,048,576 keys, top-k 2048, GB300) FE top-k took 22.75 ms on BF16 scores versus 14.45 ms on FP32 scores, although it reads half the bytes; with this change BF16 takes 13.35 ms. This is what makes BF16 dense indexer scores (the separate BF16-scores PR) usable with FE's own top-k.

Exactness: BF16 -> FP32 is exact and FP32 -> FP16 round-to-nearest is monotonic (saturating to inf above 65504), so the coarse bins never reorder the exact keys (checked exhaustively over all non-NaN BF16 values by `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_bf16_fp16_coarse_bins`). Elements in bins before the threshold bin are strictly larger than every threshold-bin element, and the threshold bin is resolved on the exact 16-bit key, so the selected set, `tie_break` and deterministic mode are unchanged in meaning. The FP16 zero bin and the two saturated bins span many BF16 exponents, which is why both refine bytes are needed (the same test asserts it).

### Hard Rules notes (`python/cudnn/AGENTS.md`)

- Rule 1 / Rule 8: the scratch stays caller-owned; `scratch_workspace_bytes()` reports the larger size for wide BF16 and `execute()` still validates, never allocates.
- Rule 2: same single kernel launch (per int32-indexable row chunk, as before).
- Rule 4: the choice depends only on the dtype and the bucketed column count, both already in the compile key.
- Rule 7: no new CuTe DSL API (`BFloat16.to(Float32)`, `Float32.to(Float16)`); tested on 4.6.2.

## Related issues

None filed. Pairs with the BF16 dense indexer scores change (`indexer_forward_wrapper(..., out_dtype=torch.bfloat16)`, a separate PR from the same author), whose GB300 measurements found FE top-k slower on BF16 than on FP32 at 1M keys. The two PRs are independent.

## API and compatibility impact

- `buffer_numbers` (kernel module helper) gains a trailing `num_cols=None`; positional callers keep working and get the dtype's maximum, which is safe (over-provisioned) for every width.
- `IndexerTopK.scratch_workspace_bytes()` doubles for BF16 inputs wider than 32,768 columns (now equal to FP32's: `n_rows * 2 * num_cols * 4`). Callers that size the workspace from `scratch_workspace_bytes()` or use `indexer_top_k_wrapper` need no change; a caller that hard-coded one scratch row for BF16 gets the existing "undersized workspace" error before launch. At 1M keys and Megatron's 1024-row chunks the BF16 top-k peak above the scores goes from 4.19 to 8.19 GiB (FP32: 8.25 GiB).
- Performance: BF16 rows wider than 32,768 columns only; see Testing for where it is faster and where it is slower.
- Architectures unchanged (SM90+); SM120 shared-memory limits and the deterministic-mode column limits are unchanged.

## Testing

`test/python/deepseek_sparse_attention/cutedsl/`:

- `dsa_utils.py`, `DSA_INDEXER_TOP_K_PARAM_MARKS` (used by `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_compile_execute` and `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_wrapper`), two new `L0` rows x `tie_break` 0/1/2 x `return_val`:
  - `bf16-wide-k2048`: adversarial patterns (ties, constant rows, +-0, adjacent representable values, inf, -inf padding) at 65,536 columns, `next_n=2` (speculative stagger, short and K-boundary rows); the constant rows put all 65,536 candidates into one bin, so both candidate buffers fill shared memory and spill.
  - `bf16-wide-random-k2048`: 1024 random rows x 131,072 columns (UINT32 indices, large-occupancy spill).
- `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_bf16_wide_rows_use_fp16_coarse_key`: for FP32/FP16/BF16 and widths 1024 ... 1M, the kernel's coarse-key choice, refine rounds, buffer count and `buffer_numbers()` agree; `scratch_workspace_bytes()` at 32,768 vs 32,769 BF16 columns.
- `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_bf16_fp16_coarse_bins`: exhaustive over all non-NaN BF16 values: the FP16-derived coarse key is monotone in the exact key; the zero and saturated bins hold several top bytes.
- `test_DSA_indexer_top_k_bf16_wide_rows_exact[ties-none, ties-small, ties-large, deterministic, deterministic-large]`: 100,003 columns (odd width: misaligned row starts), random BF16 bit patterns whose cutoff lands in the saturated +inf bin, the -inf bin, the zero and -0 bins, the FP16 subnormal bins and the top normal bin, plus exact-multiplicity ties at the cutoff inside the +inf and zero bins; full and ragged row lengths; checked against `ref_indexer_top_k` (sets for `tie_break` 1/2 and deterministic, values otherwise), plus ascending order and bitwise repeatability in deterministic mode.

GB300 (AWS-CMH, 1 node, 4x GB300 SM103, driver 580.159.03, CUDA 13.2, torch 2.12.0a0 nv26.04, Python 3.12, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, cuDNN backend 9.21.0; this branch's `python/cudnn` with the FE 1.31.0 aarch64 binary extension, whose required pybind symbols are unchanged; not a supported build):

| Job | Tree | `pytest -m L0 test_DSA_indexer_top_k.py` |
|---|---|---|
| 4682004 | this kernel, tests without the two coarse-bin rows of `_bf16_wide_rows` and the coarse-bin test | 170 passed, 9 skipped (SM120-only), 0 failed |
| 4682273 | this commit (inputs hash-checked against the commit) | 171 passed, 9 skipped (SM120-only), 0 failed; the 31 new cases all pass |

### Numbers (CUDA-graph replay, median of 10 replays, FE top-k with `return_val=True`, `tie_break=0`, Megatron's chunking: 8 GiB scratch budget at 2 int32 per column -> 1024 rows per launch at 1M)

Same node, same job (4682273); "develop" is unmodified develop (`4f175f3f`) in the same process layout:

| case | FP32 develop | FP32 this PR | BF16 develop | BF16 this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| S3 1M CP64 rank 0, Gaussian Q/K/W | 14.44 | 14.45 | 22.75 | **13.35** |
| S3, outlier channels | - | 14.43 | - | **13.14** |
| S4 128K CP32 rank 0, Gaussian | 0.60 | 0.59 | 0.69 | **0.56** |

Scores: develop's dense indexer scorer in FP32 on the exact GLM-5.2 geometry (32 heads x 128, THD causal segments, 8.07e9 in-row scores for S3), BF16 = the FP32 scores `.to(torch.bfloat16)` (bit-identical to the BF16 scorer's output). Job 4682004 measured the same S3 numbers (FP32 14.42, BF16 13.31, develop BF16 22.74 ms); an integer variant of the coarse key (the same bins computed from the BF16 bits instead of `cvt`) was no faster (13.30 ms).

4096 rows of `torch.randn`, all columns valid (the native BF16 key's crowding depends on where the cutoff falls among its two-binade bins):

| width | FP32 | BF16 develop | BF16 this PR |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32,768 (unchanged path) | 0.36 | 0.43 | 0.43 |
| 65,536 | 0.62 | 0.80 | **0.58** |
| 131,072 | 1.08 | **0.89** | 1.01 |
| 262,144 | 2.23 | **1.79** | 1.97 |

For plain Gaussian rows at 128K/256K the cutoff happens to fall into a sparse native BF16 bin, and the native key is 10-13% faster there; with the FP16-derived key BF16 always stays at or below FP32, while the native key's cost depends on the data (up to 1.58x FP32 at 1M above).

### Correctness at scale

On every S3 / S3-outlier / S4 row (16384 / 16384 / 4096 rows, 14080 / 14080 / 2048 of them longer than k), the BF16 selection was compared with the FP32 path's selection of the same values upcast to FP32: `tie_break=1`, `tie_break=2` and `deterministic=True` select identical sets (deterministic: ascending order too), `tie_break=0` selects the same value multiset; returned values equal the BF16 scores at the returned indices bit for bit; no duplicates; `-1` padding exact. 24 sampled long rows per case also match `ref_indexer_top_k` (and so does the FP32 reference). 0 mismatches in all three jobs.

Not run: SM90 (no Hopper), SM100 (B200), SM120 (the native SM120 tests skip on SM103; the SM120 shared-memory budget argument is above), a supported (non-hybrid) develop build, other suites (no other code path changes; `qsa_select` calls the top-k on FP32 scores).

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- For coarse bins inside FP16's normal and subnormal range the first (top-byte) refine round is degenerate: such a bin holds one BF16 exponent. Skipping it based on the threshold bin was exact but measured slower (S3 BF16 14.94 ms vs 13.35 ms), presumably from the dynamic shift/loop bound in the hot collect pass; worth revisiting together with FP32, whose first round is degenerate for the same bins.
- At 1M keys FP32 and BF16 now take about the same time (14.4 vs 13.4 ms) although BF16 reads half the bytes, so the kernel is bound by per-element work (the shared-memory histogram atomics) rather than bandwidth; DeepSelect's BF16 top-k takes 4.0 ms on the same rows.

For the QSA request, I checked the supplied Relax selector at `d16f2e3ec45be059db6377295090b1d49257892c`. Its BF16 indexer GEMM produces FP32 scores, and top-k consumes FP32 after ReLU/head reduction. At 128K tokens with four-token blocks, the candidate width is at most 32,768. This PR changes BF16 rows wider than 32,768, so it does not accelerate that exact selector path. Converting scores to BF16 would be a separate numerical/selection change requiring exact-set and training validation.

I would keep this draft scoped to its demonstrated wide-BF16 workload. Before approval, qualify the intended supported build and decide/document admission for the measured 128K/256K Gaussian regressions and larger scratch requirement. This is a scope assessment for the QSA handoff, not a full kernel approval.

@@ -86,7 +86,7 @@ def _make_call(scores, lengths, k, deterministic, ordering="auto"):
     )
     buffer = torch.empty(
         rows,
-        topk_kernel.buffer_numbers(scores.dtype),
+        topk_kernel.buffer_numbers(scores.dtype, cols),
         cols,
         dtype=torch.int32,
         device=scores.device,

@@ -513,8 +513,9 @@ is `(n_rows, top_k)` in the input dtype, both contiguous and on `input_values`'
 device. `out_values` is required when the object was built with

For the QSA request, I checked the supplied Relax selector at `d16f2e3ec45be059db6377295090b1d49257892c`. Its BF16 indexer GEMM produces FP32 scores, and top-k consumes FP32 after ReLU/head reduction. At 128K tokens with four-token blocks, the candidate width is at most 32,768. This PR changes BF16 rows wider than 32,768, so it does not accelerate that exact selector path. Converting scores to BF16 would be a separate numerical/selection change requiring exact-set and training validation.

I would keep this draft scoped to its demonstrated wide-BF16 workload. Before approval, qualify the intended supported build and decide/document admission for the measured 128K/256K Gaussian regressions and larger scratch requirement. This is a scope assessment for the QSA handoff, not a full kernel approval.

— Codex (gpt-6-astra), acting on Yang Xu's requested QSA investigation
